Q: How can I transition to Software Development/Engineering? A:

Getting a job in this field is tough right now. I was in your boat for a long time. I must have applied to a billion roles but really what it comes down to is this: a lot of experience in the field and a lot of timing. Most jobs will require you to have unrealistic "x years of experience". The point is to simply get into the Software Engineering field. Get some job that has even 30% of what you want to do, then you will job hop (the economy is incentivizing you to job-hop every couple of years to salary increase). But you can be a bit more picky on your second job, and third, and so on. Don't be picky on your first job. You can't be. You're competing against a vast pool of people who are lying on their resumes, who are truly more experienced than you, and so on...

PS: what helped me a lot is targeted resumes. I got interviews quickly that way.

Q: Groovy - get JAVA_HOME from program A:

A gotcha that bit me. Remember to use curly braces inside a gstring.

println "inside a gstring, java.home=$System.properties.'java.home' will be problematic

//dumps all system properties

but

println "inside a gstring, java.home=${System.properties.'java.home'} will be fine

Result: inside a gstring, java.home=C:\FAST\JDK64\1.7.0.79\jre will be fine

Q: How do I ensure that whitespace is preserved in Markdown? A:

I find   very cumbersome to use, i.e. if you have large document, it may become ugly in regards to editing, and you would need lots of copy pasting of  . In the end, you will also need to adjust indentation.

Instead, use three grave accents (```) to denote code, or in your case, indentation and whitespace.

For example, this is how text looks without any formatting:

Enabled = "True"

Profile = ("Domain", "Private")

Direction = "OutBound"

RemotePort = ("8080", "8081")

LocalPort = ("9080", "9081")

This is how it looks with   doing quick copy paste:

Enabled      = "True"

Profile      = ("Domain", "Private")

Direction      = "OutBound"

RemotePort      = ("8080", "8081")

LocalPort      = ("9080", "9081")

My solution, using grave accents:

Enabled               = "True"
Profile               = ("Domain", "Private")
Direction             = "OutBound"
RemotePort            = ("8080", "8081")
LocalPort             = ("9080", "9081")

The Markdown code in the last example is surrounded by three backticks (grave accents) at the beginning and at the end. Example:

```
your text here
```

Q: Does npx no longer do install-less run? A:

Notwithstanding the "Need to install the following packages … Ok to proceed?" prompt, it would appear that npx is only "installing" the package in the cache (as apparently it always has).

As of npx 11.19.0 on Windows 11, you can afterward see that the package is not installed globally:

npm ls -g

You should be able to find the cached "installed" package in %LocalAppData%\npm-cache\_npx (on Windows).

On the positive side, this provides more feedback that something is being saved. On the negative side, the message is misleading; it should say something like "Need to cache the following package …".

Q: (When) should I use type hinting in PHP? A:

Actually, if you think you want to use type hinting, you should first check to see if you are using the best language. Maybe it's time to switch from PHP to Java (static typing) or to one of Ruby, Python, or JavaScript via Node.js (pure dynamic languages, no interfaces or type checking). All languages mentioned above support annotations, which are useful in their own right. And all of them except PHP make the choice for you. You will either use types, or you won't. There's no middle ground. And that can be very freeing.

But if you stick with PHP, you are going to have to make decisions about which way you want to go. To answer your question, you should use type hints when you want more help from the IDE. That's it. Otherwise, I wouldn't bother with them. Why? Because use of type hints is unenforceable and gains you nothing when there is no mandated compile step. It gains you some idea of correctness as you code since your IDE will flag stuff. I know that maybe you can use tooling before code is committed or deployed to block those steps if there's a type problem, and so maybe you can do some enforcement that way. But you will never truly be forced to otherwise and once you start adding tooling and more steps, you lose rapid iteration, one of PHP's core strengths.

For safety, with or without static typing or type hints, you still obviously need to test your code. Unit and integration tests are still needed for all mentioned languages. As many know, all languages can suffer runtime errors. Yes, even Java, for all its static typing. You can get null pointer exceptions, class cast exceptions, runtime reflection problems, and so forth. Java gives you static typing for safety at compile time but it's not a silver bullet end to end. In PHP, type hints are even less of a silver bullet. So I suggest adding them for IDE help and not for safety. Safety is more the domain of testing anyway. This approach might be controversial, but I think it's the pragmatic way to go about things in 2026 if you insist on sticking with PHP. With PHP, the added burden on the developer is exactly this question, every time you touch PHP code. With the other languages, this question doesn't come up at all.

Q: How to one data file upload into multiple table by sql loader in oracle 10g example A:

You can use a single control file to load data into more than one tables using SQLLDR. What you need to keep in mind is, 

 LOAD DATA
    INFILE   '/image/ExtTableData/OnlineClaims/member_master.csv'
    TRUNCATE
    INTO TABLE EMP
    FIELDS TERMINATED BY "," 
TRAILING NULLCOLS
    (ID POSITION(1),
      NAME,
      HIRE_DATE,
      DEPARTMENT_ID
    )
    INTO TABLE EMP_EPFO
    (EMP_ID POSITION(1),
     LNAME,
     HIRE_DATE,
     DEPT_ID
     )

The reason for specifying POSITION(1) after the columns for separate tables is to instruct Oracle to start reading data from first row.

Quoting from Oracle documentation:

When the POSITION parameter is not used, multiple INTO TABLE clauses process different parts of the same (delimited data) input record, allowing multiple tables to be loaded from one record. When the POSITION parameter is used, multiple INTO TABLE clauses can process the same record in different ways, allowing multiple formats to be recognized in one input file.
